newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Allianz Life sees tax woes easing.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Allianz Life sees tax woes easing.

text.p: Allianz Leben, Germany's top life insurer, on Friday posted below-plan growth for the first half of 1997 but said it was optimistic for the second half after Bonn failed to push through proposals for a tax on life insurance income.

Allianz Lebensversicherungs AG, the life arm of the giant Allianz AG group, said public concern over the tax debate meant its new business grew by only 6.7 percent to 1.3 billion marks in the period to June 30, slowing from the year-ago period.
But the company said it expected " an overall satisfactory business development" for 1997.

Sunnier conditions are ahead for the insurance industry after controversial government plans to tax life insurance investment income were defeated late last month along with a whole package of sweeping tax reforms.
In addition, the company said it had launched several sales incentives related to its 75th anniversary which should translate into good sales.
"Allianz Leben is expecting a stronger pick-up in new business in the second half," the insurer said in its interim report.
Total premium income rose 5.1 percent to six billion marks in the first half and total sums insured advanced 5.2 percent to 297 billion marks.
Payouts to customers, including redeemed policies, rose by 7.5 percent to 4.3 billion marks.

Allianz Leben said its investments were helped by strong market conditions. Low interest rates cut income from deposits but stock market gains compensated. Capital investments advanced 8.2 percent to 123.7 billion marks.

Allianz Leben, in a brief reference to the massive class action lawsuit launched against it and other insurers in the U.S., also noted that its investigation of its files from the Nazi era had not yet been completed.

Allianz is among 16 insurers embroiled in a legal tussle over missing Holocaust funds. The lawsuit brought by Holocaust victims and their descendents alleges that insurers cheated Nazi victims of billions of dollars.

The company, while stressing that it believes most claims have already been settled, has pledged to honour all reasonable claims related to the Nazi period and is running a 24-hour hotline to enable people to state their cases.
Lawyers representing claimants earlier this week protested that Allianz had been given access to government files on the Nazi era which they had been denied.
